passage:
"Get away from me!" Irfan shouted, knocking his chair over when the balloon popped behind him.
"Everyone, please move to the reading corner," Ms Rashmi said evenly. "Meher, take the group with you."
"He threw a chair, Miss! Aren't you going to punish him?"
"Right now I'm making sure everyone is safe. We'll talk about the chair later."
She crouched a few steps from Irfan, not too close. "Irfan, you're breathing really fast. That bang scared your body. You're safe here."
"I thought something exploded," Irfan whispered, shaking.
"That sounds really frightening. Can you breathe out slowly with me?"
Later, when he was calm, they picked up the chair together.
"Tomorrow let's talk about what to do when a noise scares you," she said.

qa.q: What made Irfan shout and knock his chair over?
qa.a: The balloon popped behind Irfan.

qa.q: How did Ms Rashmi feel during the moment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ms Rashmi felt calm and focused on safety; she spoke evenly, moved the class away and put off the talk about the chair.

qa.q: Why did Ms Rashmi move the class before talking about the chair?
qa.a: Safety and calm had to come first; Irfan could not think about consequences while scared, so the chair was dealt with later, together.

qa.q: What was the balloon pop like for Irfan?
qa.a: For Irfan it felt like real danger; he thought something had exploded, and his body reacted before he could think.

grounding: A teacher reads a child's sudden aggression as a fear reaction, putting safety and calm first and leaving consequences for later.

passage: I'm Manjula, and I still remember the morning I nearly got it wrong. The principal was shouting at some older boys in the corridor. When I turned round, Kiran was under his desk, knees pulled up. My first thought was, not now, Kiran. Then I saw how pale he was. I knelt and said, "You're safe. Stay there as long as you need." When he came out, he kept saying, "Sorry, Miss. I'll be good, I'll clean the board, I'll do anything." He was far too eager. I told him he wasn't in trouble. I'd half wanted to scold him for leaving his seat, but that could wait. Later that week we talked calmly about where he could sit when noises get loud.

qa.q: Where was Kiran when Manjula turned round?
qa.a: Kiran was under his desk, knees pulled up.

qa.q: What did Manjula feel at first, and what changed her mind?
qa.a: Manjula first felt impatient, thinking "not now, Kiran", but seeing how pale he was made her realise he was scared.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Manjula to leave the talk about his seat until later?
qa.a: Kiran needed to feel safe first; a scolding while he was scared would only add fear, so a calm talk later that week could actually help.

qa.q: Why might Kiran have become so eager to please after coming out?
qa.a: Kiran was likely still frightened by the shouting, and being extra good may have felt like a way to stay safe from anger.

grounding: A teacher recognises a child's hiding and sudden over-eagerness as stress reactions, keeps him safe first and leaves the discussion for later.

passage:
Class 4B incident note, Friday
The fire drill siren went off without warning at 11:10. Most of the class lined up. Mehak dived under her desk and wrapped her arms round her knees. When Karan reached down to pull her out, she kicked at his hand and screamed. I sent the others out with the class monitor and the teacher from next door, then crouched beside her desk, keeping my voice low. 'It's a practice. Nothing is burning. I'm staying right here.' I did not mention the kick. After some minutes her breathing slowed and she let me walk her out, holding my sleeve. Later, once she was calm, we talked about Karan's hand and she said sorry to him herself. I have told her parents and the counsellor, and next time I will warn her before a drill.
Yogesh Rao, class teacher

qa.q: What time did the siren go off?
What was Yogesh thinking when choosing not to mention the kick straight away?
qa.a: Yogesh was concerned that Mehak was terrified rather than naughty, and wanted her to feel safe and calm before any talk about the kick.

qa.q: What could the school change before the next drill?
qa.a: Warn Mehak before a drill, as Yogesh plans, so the siren does not come as a shock.

qa.q: How might Karan have experienced the kick?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to help, and her apology later may have eased that.

grounding: Shows a teacher recognising a child's hiding and sudden aggression as a stress reaction, putting safety and calm first and discussing the kick later.

passage:
Wednesday night
Something about Sabina today unsettled me. Normally she argues about everything. Today it was 'Yes, Lakshmi Miss, sorry, Lakshmi Miss' all morning. When Aman bumped her tray at lunch, she apologised to him. She offered to clean the board, collect the books, stay in at break. And every few seconds her eyes flicked to my face. It took me till the afternoon to connect it with yesterday, when I lost my temper and shouted at the whole class about the noise. She isn't being good. She's scared of me. After the last bell I asked her to help me water the class plants, just the two of us. I said, 'I shouted too loudly yesterday. I'm sorry. You don't have to keep me happy.' Her shoulders dropped a little. Tomorrow I'll ask the counsellor for ideas, and I'm keeping my voice down.

qa.q: What did Sabina offer to do during the day?
qa.a: Clean the board, collect the books and stay in at break.

qa.q: What did the diary writer feel on realising why Sabina was so agreeable?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt unsettled and guilty, realising Sabina was scared after yesterday's shouting.

qa.q: What small step did Lakshmi take once the pattern was clear?
qa.a: Lakshmi gave Sabina a calm, private job, apologised for shouting and told her she did not have to keep Lakshmi happy.

qa.q: What might the day have been like for Sabina?
qa.a: It may have felt tense and tiring, watching Lakshmi's face all day and trying to stay on her good side to feel safe.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a child's sudden, unnatural agreeableness is a fear reaction, restoring calm first and planning next steps later.

passage: The truck outside the school in Kotwa backfired with a bang like a gun. In the one-room classroom, eight-year-old Siddharth leapt up, threw his slate across the floor and shoved the boy beside him off the mat. Then he stood shaking, fists raised, eyes huge. A few children laughed nervously. Rehana, the teacher, did not raise her voice. She moved the other boy to the far side, told the class to start copying the next line, and knelt a little distance from Siddharth. 'Just a truck, Siddharth. You're safe. Sit down when you're ready.' She handed him her steel tumbler of water. His fists slowly opened. The next morning, when he was calm, she sat with him on the step and talked about the shove, and he helped pick up the other boy's scattered chalks.

qa.q: What made the bang outside the school?
qa.a: The truck outside the school backfired.

qa.q: What did Rehana seem to feel as she watched Siddharth shake with raised fists?
qa.a: She seemed steady and calm, and concerned for him, reading his shove as fright rather than naughtiness.

qa.q: Why did Rehana wait until the next morning to talk about the shove?
qa.a: Talking while Siddharth was still frightened would not help; once he was calm he could listen, understand and make amends.

qa.q: How might the boy who was shoved see what happened?
qa.a: He may have felt startled and hurt, and waiting until Siddharth was calm made a real apology more likely.

grounding: Shows a teacher recognising sudden aggression as a stress reaction to a loud bang, putting safety and calm first and discussing consequences the next day.

passage: When the fire-drill bell shrieked in the Valencia primary school, most of Camila's class lined up, grumbling. Mei did not. She shoved her chair over, kicked at a boy who touched her arm, then crawled under her desk, knees to her chest. A colleague at the door called, 'Mei! Out, now, or it's detention!' Camila held up a hand and knelt by the desk. 'Mei, it's a practice. You're safe. I'm staying right here.' She waited until Mei's breathing slowed, then walked out with her, holding her hand. Only the next day, calmly, did they talk about the kick, and Camila told the school counsellor so they could plan for the next drill.

qa.q: Where did Mei crawl?
qa.a: Under her desk.

qa.q: How did Camila feel on seeing Mei under the desk?
qa.a: Camila felt concerned and understood that the kicking and hiding were fear reactions to the shrieking bell, not defiance.

qa.q: Why did Camila wait until the next day to talk about the kick?
qa.a: Safety and calm came first; once Mei was settled, a calm talk about consequences could actually be heard.

qa.q: What was the fire drill like for Mei?
qa.a: For Mei the bell probably felt like real danger, so her body fought and hid before she could think.

grounding: A teacher recognises a child's sudden aggression and hiding as stress reactions and puts safety and calm before consequences.
